title: Prenatal exposure to perfluorooctanoate (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS) and maternally reported developmental milestones in infancy.
ehr_evidence: We obtained data on Apgar scores by linking cohort members to the National Hospital Discharge Register (Copenhagen, Denmark) through use of the unique personal identification number assigned to all Danish residents at birth or immigration.
summary: A prospective study within the Danish National Birth Cohort of 1,400 mother-child pairs examining associations between first-trimester maternal plasma PFOA/PFOS levels and child developmental milestones (motor and mental) and Apgar scores.
key_findings: No significant association between maternal plasma PFOA or PFOS levels and Apgar score; OR for Apgar score < 10 (fourth vs first quartile) was 1.20 (95% CI, 0.67–2.14) for PFOS and 1.14 (95% CI, 0.57–2.25) for PFOA after adjustment.
No significant associations between PFOA or PFOS levels and the age at which children could walk without support.

Higher maternal PFOS levels were associated with a later age of sitting without support; adjusted HRs 0.85 (95% CI, 0.72–0.99) for the third quartile and 0.86 (95% CI, 0.73–1.01) for the fourth quartile versus the first quartile (p for trend = 0.041).
Higher maternal PFOS (but not PFOA) levels were associated with higher odds of infants not using word-like sounds (OR for fourth vs first quartile = 2.93; 95% CI, 1.00–8.56; p for trend = 0.04).
No associations between PFC exposure and motor or mental development were observed at the 6-month interview.
captured_features: First-trimester maternal plasma PFOA and PFOS concentrations (ng/mL)
Apgar score (from National Hospital Discharge Register)
Motor developmental milestones (sitting and walking without support)
Mental developmental milestones (language, cognition, attention, social-personal)
Covariates: maternal age, parity, education, occupation, prepregnancy BMI, smoking, alcohol consumption, breast-feeding, out-of-home child care, home density, child's sex
study_design: Prospective cohort (study within the Danish National Birth Cohort)
population: 1,400 mother-child pairs from the Danish National Birth Cohort; women recruited in early pregnancy (1996–2002); children assessed at ~6 and ~18 months of age
limitations: Maternal blood measured early in pregnancy may not reflect critical fetal brain exposures throughout pregnancy and early childhood.
Reliance on maternal self-report for developmental milestones introduces potential measurement error, though nondifferential.
Residual confounding by childhood exposure variables (breast-feeding, household exposure) cannot be ruled out.
PFOA and PFOS levels were correlated (r = 0.62), limiting mutual adjustment.
Small number of infants with low Apgar scores limits precision of that outcome.
